prompt: A beginner asks whether a Hugging Face token pays for local training. Answer in one sentence.
chosen: No. The token only authenticates model or dataset access and optional uploads; training compute comes from your local NVIDIA GPU.
rejected: Yes. Hugging Face uses the token to provide the GPU that runs your local training job.

prompt: Recommend a safe first configuration for an 8 GB NVIDIA GPU.
chosen: Start with a small model such as Qwen3 0.6B, QLoRA, Auto compute, and the Smoke preset, then measure memory before scaling up.
rejected: Start with the largest available model, FP32, maximum sequence length, and the Quality preset so the first result is definitive.

prompt: Explain what a completed PEFT adapter needs at inference time.
chosen: It needs the compatible base model and revision plus the adapter and tokenizer files; the adapter is not a standalone model.
rejected: Nothing else is needed because the adapter contains a complete copy of every base-model weight.

prompt: The training loss decreased. State what can be concluded.
chosen: The model predicts the training objective better; held-out evaluation is still required before claiming better real-world behavior.
rejected: The model is now proven more factual, safer, and better on every unseen prompt.

prompt: A dataset has 900 rows from source A and 100 from source B. Describe this app's mixing behavior.
chosen: The app concatenates and shuffles the rows, so source A contributes about nine times as many examples unless the data is balanced beforehand.
rejected: The app automatically oversamples source B until both sources contribute exactly half of every batch.

prompt: Differentiate gradient checkpointing from a disk training checkpoint.
chosen: Gradient checkpointing recomputes activations to save VRAM; a disk checkpoint saves training state so an interrupted run can resume.
rejected: They are two names for the same file that stores a backup copy of GPU memory.

prompt: A user needs frequently changing private facts with citations. Recommend the first technique to test.
chosen: Test retrieval-augmented generation first, because it can fetch current authorized sources without encoding changing facts into model weights.
rejected: Fine-tune the facts permanently into the model and rely on it to cite the exact source later.

prompt: Explain why closing the browser tab may not stop training.
chosen: Training runs in a separate worker process, so use the app's verified cancellation or shutdown control when you intend to stop it.
rejected: The browser owns the CUDA process, so closing any tab always terminates training immediately.

prompt: A user wants to enable Unsloth with QOFT on Linux. Give the current app limitation.
chosen: This integration supports Unsloth only on native Windows and only for LoRA or QLoRA; Linux QOFT uses the standard backend.
rejected: Enable the toggle anyway because Unsloth supports every method and platform exposed by the app.

prompt: Describe the purpose of the Smoke preset.
chosen: It cheaply verifies that data, model loading, training, status, and artifact paths work; it is not evidence of production quality.
rejected: It is the recommended final production configuration because 20 steps guarantee convergence.

prompt: A user gets CUDA out-of-memory during a first run. Give a conservative response.
chosen: Use a smaller model, QLoRA, shorter sequences, and the smallest valid batch, keep checkpointing enabled, and close other GPU applications.
rejected: Disable validation and retry repeatedly without changing the model, sequence length, batch, or competing GPU processes.

prompt: Explain why preference labels need a written rubric.
chosen: A rubric makes chosen and rejected judgments consistent, reviewable, and tied to the behavior the project claims to improve.
rejected: A rubric is unnecessary because any personal preference creates an objective quality label.

prompt: State the relationship between QLoRA and DPO.
chosen: QLoRA is a parameter and memory method, while DPO is a preference-training objective; they can be selected together but are different axes.
rejected: They are competing names for the same loss function, so selecting one automatically disables the other.

prompt: A reward-model run completed. Explain why the current Monitor does not compare generated answers.
chosen: The reward adapter produces scalar preference scores through a sequence-classification head, while the comparison UI is built for causal text generation.
rejected: Reward models cannot be evaluated in any way after training.

prompt: A user asks whether GPU cache cleanup can free another application's VRAM.
chosen: No. It releases only unused cache owned by the current PyTorch process, not live tensors or memory owned by workers, Ollama, or other applications.
rejected: Yes. The cleanup button clears all allocations on the physical GPU regardless of which process owns them.

prompt: Recommend how to compare two training configurations.
chosen: Keep the model, data, seed, and evaluation fixed, change one primary variable, and record the hypothesis before running.
rejected: Change the model, dataset, learning rate, epochs, and method together, then attribute any difference to the setting you prefer.

prompt: A user wants to upload an adapter to the Hub. Name two checks before publishing.
chosen: Verify the destination and token permissions, and review model/data licenses, privacy, access level, and the adapter's documented limitations.
rejected: Publish first because adapters never contain behavior learned from the training data and have no licensing concerns.

prompt: Explain why an installed TRL trainer does not automatically mean the app supports that approach.
chosen: The app also needs a dataset contract, validation, model path, controls, artifacts, evaluation behavior, tests, and documentation.
rejected: Import success is sufficient; every trainer can safely reuse the SFT form and dataset without other changes.

prompt: Define a test-set contamination failure.
chosen: Training on test examples or tuning repeatedly to their results makes the final score an unreliable estimate of unseen performance.
rejected: Using test examples during training improves the reliability of the final unbiased evaluation.

prompt: A user asks whether FP32 always produces a better adapter than BF16.
chosen: No. FP32 costs much more VRAM and time, while adapter quality depends on data, objective, optimization, and hardware stability; evaluate rather than assume.
rejected: Yes. Doubling precision always improves downstream quality enough to justify the memory cost.
